title: Getting Started
objectives: Explain source code, compilation and executables, including why changing source does not update an existing executable.
Write `fn main() { }` and identify the program's entry point.
Print exact text, using `println!` to end a line and `print!` to continue it.
Use positional `{}` and supplied inline `{name}` placeholders, and print literal braces with `{{` and `}}`.
Recognise a macro call by `!` and read a compiler diagnostic's location and suggested fix.
Read and edit package name, version and edition in `Cargo.toml`, and recognise `[dependencies]`.
Choose between `cargo new`, `cargo build`, `cargo run` and `cargo check`, and locate source and generated output.

lessons.title: What a program is, and what Rust is for
lessons.book_section: 1.1 Installation; 1.2 Compilation and Execution (adapted for app onboarding)
lessons.objective_md: After this lesson the learner can say what a program, source code, a compiler and an executable are, describe the path from `main.rs` to a running program with `rustc`, and say what kind of software Rust is used for.

screens.heading: A program is a list of instructions
screens.text_md:
A **program** is a list of instructions for a computer. This one has three instructions. Each one prints a line of text.

Think of a recipe: "crack two eggs, whisk them, heat the pan". Each step is simple. Together they make breakfast.

The computer does exactly what the instructions say. It never guesses what you meant.

screens.heading: The computer follows the steps in order

steps.caption_md: The program starts at the top. The first instruction prints `Crack two eggs.`
steps.visual_md: Output panel shows one line: `Crack two eggs.` (the new line flashes yellow)

steps.caption_md: Then the next instruction runs. The computer always goes one step at a time, in order.
steps.visual_md: Output panel shows `Crack two eggs.` and, below it, `Whisk them.` (new line flashes yellow)

steps.caption_md: The last instruction prints `Heat the pan.`
steps.visual_md: Output panel shows the three lines `Crack two eggs.`, `Whisk them.`, `Heat the pan.` (new line flashes yellow)

steps.caption_md: At the closing `}` there is nothing left to do, so the program ends. Swap two lines and the output order swaps too.
steps.visual_md: Output panel shows the same three lines; a grey badge "Program finished" appears under them

screens.visual_md: Code stepper (code on the left; on the right a dark "Output" panel that shows each printed line as it appears)

screens.heading: Source code is text for people
screens.text_md:
What you just read is **source code**: plain text that people write and read.

A computer's processor can't run text like this. It only understands **machine code**: long lists of numbers.

So something must translate your text into machine code. For Rust, that translator is called a **compiler**, and its name is `rustc`.
screens.visual_md: three boxes left to right joined by arrows: a rust-coloured box "`main.rs` · source code · text you write", an arrow labelled "translate", a blue box "`rustc` · the compiler", an arrow, and a green box "`main` · executable · machine code the processor runs".

screens.heading: Compile first, then run

code.text:
$ rustc main.rs
$ ./main
Crack two eggs.
Whisk them.
Heat the pan.

steps.caption_md: You ask the compiler to translate your file: `rustc main.rs`.
steps.visual_md: `main.rs` box has a rust border and is lit; `rustc` and `main` boxes are greyed out

steps.caption_md: `rustc` reads the **whole** file and checks it for mistakes before it translates anything.
steps.visual_md: `rustc` box lit with a blue border and the badge "checking…"; `main.rs` box normal; `main` box still greyed out

steps.caption_md: If everything checks out, `rustc` writes a new file: an **executable** called `main` (`main.exe` on Windows).
steps.visual_md: `main` box appears lit with a green border and the badge "new file"; arrow into it turns green

steps.caption_md: Now you run the executable with `./main` (PowerShell: `.\main.exe`). It prints the three lines. You can run it again and again without compiling again.
steps.visual_md: `main` box has the badge "running"; the other two boxes are normal

screens.visual_md: Code stepper (the three boxes from screen 3 light up one at a time)

options.text_md: It runs the instructions in `main.rs` one by one, right away.
It checks `main.rs` and translates it into an executable file.
It opens `main.rs` so you can edit it.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. `rustc` doesn't run your program. It produces an executable, and you run that file in a separate step with `./main`.
Correct. `rustc` is the compiler: it checks the source code and, if there are no errors, writes an executable.
Not quite. Editing happens in a text editor. `rustc` only reads the file to translate it.
Not quite. The compiler works entirely on your own computer. Nothing is sent anywhere.

screens.heading: The compiler checks before anything runs
screens.text_md:
Line 3 is missing its semicolon. This build fails and creates no new executable. The compiler points to the missing semicolon.

Compiling does not run any of these print calls. If an older executable exists, it stays unchanged; it does not contain your latest edits.

Compiler messages are your friend. Read them slowly: what went wrong, where, and how to fix it.
screens.diagnostic:
error: expected `;`, found `println`
 --> src/main.rs:3:28
  |
3 |     println!("Whisk them.")
  |                            ^ help: add `;` here
4 |     println!("Heat the pan.");
  |     ------- unexpected token

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

annotations.note_md: line 3, column 28: the end of line 3, where the `;` is missing.
the compiler even suggests the fix.
this build creates no new executable and runs none of these print calls. An executable from an earlier successful build is a separate file.

question.prompt_md: If `rustc` finds a mistake on line 3, it still produces an executable that runs lines 1 and 2.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. When there is an error, this build produces no new executable and runs none of the source instructions.
Correct. The build must pass its checks first. A failed build creates no new executable and does not run any of the source instructions.

coming_from.c: Like `gcc` or `clang`, `rustc` compiles ahead of time to a native executable. Safe Rust adds checks that prevent use-after-free, double frees and data races. You will meet ownership in Chapter 4.
coming_from.go: Like `go build`, `rustc` produces a single native executable. Unlike Go, Rust has no garbage collector; memory safety comes from checks the compiler does (Chapter 4).
coming_from.java: `javac` and the C# compiler produce bytecode that a virtual machine runs, with a garbage collector freeing memory. `rustc` produces machine code that runs directly on the processor: no virtual machine and no garbage collector.
coming_from.js: JavaScript is run by an engine that reads the source at run time; TypeScript checks types and then outputs JavaScript. `rustc` checks your code and outputs machine code directly, so no engine is needed to run it.
coming_from.python: Python usually runs through an interpreter, which may compile your source to bytecode first. Many errors are discovered during execution. Rust checks types and ownership ahead of time and produces a native executable.

screens.heading: Your Rust tools, inside the app
screens.text_md:
The app uses Rust installed on your computer. Onboarding checks for `rustc` and Cargo and guides installation with `rustup` if needed.

Once setup is complete, press **Run** to compile your code and run the visible tests locally. Nothing is uploaded.

The course targets Rust 1.98 and edition 2024. Cargo, Rust's build tool, is two lessons away.

**Source code** is text for people; the processor runs **machine code**.
The **compiler**, `rustc`, checks the whole program and translates it into an **executable**.
If this build fails, no new executable is made; compiling does not run the program.
Rust is built for fast, reliable software, and its strict compiler catches bugs early.

lessons.title: Hello, world!
lessons.objective_md: After this lesson the learner can write a `main` function, print text with `println!` and `print!` using `{}` placeholders and `{{ }}`, and explain why `println!` has a `!`.

screens.heading: Your first Rust program

steps.caption_md: Each executable in this course starts by running the function called `main`.
steps.visual_md: Output panel empty; a badge "start here" points at `main` on line 1

steps.caption_md: Inside `main` there is one instruction: print `Hello, world!` and move to a new line.
steps.visual_md: Output panel shows `Hello, world!` (flashes yellow)

steps.caption_md: The closing `}` ends `main`, and with it the program.
steps.visual_md: Output panel still shows `Hello, world!`; grey badge "Program finished" below it

screens.visual_md: Code stepper (code on the left; "Output" panel on the right)

screens.heading: Every program starts at main
screens.text_md:
`fn` declares a **function**: a named group of instructions. This one is named `main`, followed by empty parentheses `()`.

`main` is special. When the program starts, Rust runs `main` first. Each executable in this course has one entry point named `main`.

The function's **body** sits between `{` and `}`. Indenting the body by four spaces is the usual style; the compiler doesn't require it.

coming_from.c: Same role as `int main()`. Rust's `main` returns nothing by default, and there's no `#include`: `println!` is always available.
coming_from.go: Very close to `func main()` in package `main`. Rust writes `fn` instead of `func` and needs no package line.
coming_from.java: Same idea as `public static void main(String[] args)` or `static void Main()`, but Rust's `main` doesn't live in a class and needs no modifiers.
coming_from.js: JavaScript runs top-level statements as the file loads. Rust has no top-level statements that run; the program starts in `fn main()`.
coming_from.python: Python runs a file from top to bottom, and `if __name__ == "__main__":` is optional. In Rust nothing runs at the top level of a file: execution always starts in `fn main()`.

question.prompt_md: Where does a Rust program start running?

options.text_md: At the first line of the file, whatever it is.
At the first `println!` in the file.
At the last function in the file.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. That's how a Python script works. In Rust, code runs only inside functions, and the program starts in `main`.
Correct. `fn main()` is the entry point of every Rust executable.
Not quite. `println!` is just one instruction. It runs only when the function it's in runs, starting from `main`.
Not quite. The order of functions in the file doesn't matter. The program always starts in `main`.

screens.heading: println! prints a line
screens.text_md:
`println!("...")` prints the text between the quotes, then moves to a new line. The text in quotes is called a **string literal**.

These print calls end with a semicolon `;`, marking the end of each **statement**. Use that style here. Some final expressions can omit it; Chapter 3 explains when.

This program prints two lines, in order.

screens.heading: The ! means macro
screens.text_md:
The `!` in `println!` means it's a **macro**, not a normal function. A macro is code that writes more code for you when the program is compiled.

That's why `println!` can take any number of values. Each `{}` is a **placeholder**, filled by the next value after the text.

Output: `No values`, `One value: 1`, `Two values: cats and dogs`. You'll write your own macros in Chapter 20.

question.prompt_md: `println!` is a normal function call, and the `!` is only there for emphasis.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. The `!` is part of the syntax: it marks a macro call. Leaving it out is a compile error (E0423).
Correct. A name followed by `!` is a macro. Macros can take a variable number of arguments, which normal functions can't.

screens.heading: Forget the ! and the compiler tells you
screens.text_md:
Without the `!`, Rust looks for a *function* called `println`. There isn't one, only a macro.

The message has three parts: what's wrong, where (`src/main.rs:2:5` is line 2, column 5), and a suggested fix. Most Rust error messages follow this shape.
screens.diagnostic:
error[E0423]: expected function, found macro `println`
 --> src/main.rs:2:5
  |
2 |     println("Hello, world!");
  |     ^^^^^^^ not a function
  |
help: use `!` to invoke the macro
  |
2 |     println!("Hello, world!");
  |            +

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0423`.

annotations.note_md: this error has a code; `rustc --explain E0423` prints a longer explanation. Some diagnostics, such as a missing semicolon, have no error code.
points at `println` on line 2: without `!` Rust looks for a function, and there is none with that name.

annotations.mark: help: use `!` to invoke the macro

screens.heading: Put named values in your text
screens.text_md:
The first two lines give names to values. Here, `name` stands for `"Ferris"` and `legs` stands for `10`. Chapter 2 explains `let`; for now, these lines are supplied for you.

Inside the format string, `{name}` and `{legs}` insert those values. This prints `Ferris has 10 legs.`

Use a name inside braces, or use `{}` with an argument after the string.

screens.heading: print!, placeholders and braces

steps.caption_md: `print!` prints text but does **not** move to a new line. The cursor stays put.
steps.visual_md: Output: `Hello, ` with the cursor right after it, on the same line

steps.caption_md: The next `print!` continues on the same line.
steps.visual_md: Output: `Hello, world` with the cursor right after it

steps.caption_md: `println!` prints `!` and then moves to a new line. The `ln` stands for "line".
steps.visual_md: Output: `Hello, world!`; cursor now at the start of line 2

steps.caption_md: The three `{}` are filled by the three values, in order.
steps.visual_md: Output line 2: `2 + 3 = 5`; the three `{}` in the code and the values `2`, `3`, `5` are each joined by a thin arrow

steps.caption_md: To print a real brace, write it twice: `{{` prints `{` and `}}` prints `}`.
steps.visual_md: Output line 3: `Braces: {}`

screens.visual_md: Code stepper (code on the left; "Output" panel on the right with a blinking cursor showing where the next character will go)

question.general_md: `print!("ab")` stays on the line, so `println!("c")` finishes it as `abc`. The two placeholders are then filled with `d` and `e` with nothing between them.

wrong_answers.why_md: `print!` doesn't add a new line, only `println!` does.
the `{}` placeholders are replaced by the values; they aren't printed themselves.

summary: Every program starts in `fn main() { }`; the body is between the braces.
End these print statements with a semicolon `;`; Chapter 3 explains final expressions.
`println!` prints and moves to a new line; `print!` doesn't move to a new line.
`{}` uses the next argument and `{name}` uses a supplied named value; `{{` and `}}` print literal braces.
The `!` marks a **macro**. Forget it and you get error E0423.

lessons.title: Hello, Cargo!
lessons.objective_md: After this lesson the learner can create a Cargo project, name the parts of `Cargo.toml`, say what `cargo build`, `cargo run` and `cargo check` do, and say where the executable ends up.

screens.heading: Cargo builds and runs your projects
screens.text_md: `rustc` is fine for one file. Real projects have many files and use code written by other people.

coming_from.c: Cargo replaces Make or CMake plus a package manager such as vcpkg or Conan, with a standard tool used by most Rust projects.
coming_from.go: Like the `go` command: `cargo build` ≈ `go build`, `cargo run` ≈ `go run`, `Cargo.toml` ≈ `go.mod`, and `Cargo.lock` ≈ `go.sum`.
coming_from.java: Cargo is like Maven or Gradle, or the `dotnet` CLI: `Cargo.toml` ≈ `pom.xml` or a `.csproj` file, and crates.io ≈ Maven Central or NuGet.
coming_from.js: Cargo is like npm: `Cargo.toml` ≈ `package.json`, `Cargo.lock` ≈ `package-lock.json`, `cargo run` ≈ `npm start`, and crates.io ≈ the npm registry.
coming_from.python: Cargo is like pip, a virtual environment and a build step in one tool. `Cargo.toml` plays the role of `pyproject.toml`.

screens.heading: What cargo new creates

code.text:
$ cargo new hello_cargo
    Creating binary (application) `hello_cargo` package
$ cd hello_cargo

steps.caption_md: `cargo new` makes a folder called `hello_cargo` with everything a project needs. Outside an existing Git repository, Cargo normally also creates a Git repository and `.gitignore`. Git tracks file changes; it is not needed for these exercises.
steps.visual_md: Folder tree appears: `hello_cargo/`, `Cargo.toml`, `.gitignore`, `src/`, `main.rs` (indented under `src/`); all nodes plain

steps.caption_md: `Cargo.toml` describes the project: its name, version and the libraries it uses.
steps.visual_md: `Cargo.toml` node lit (rust border) with the badge "settings"

steps.caption_md: Your code goes in the `src` folder. Cargo has already written a "Hello, world!" program in `src/main.rs`.
steps.visual_md: `main.rs` node lit with the badge "your code"; below the tree a small code panel shows `fn main() { println!("Hello, world!"); }` on three lines

screens.visual_md: Code stepper (a folder tree on the right: `hello_cargo/` with children `Cargo.toml`, `.gitignore` and `src/`, and `main.rs` inside `src/`)

screens.heading: Cargo.toml describes your package
screens.text_md:
`Cargo.toml` is the project's **manifest**, written in a simple format called TOML.

`[package]` starts a section about your project: its `name`, its `version`, and the Rust `edition` it's written for.

`[dependencies]` lists other people's code that your project uses. It's empty for now; in Chapter 2 you'll add one.

code.text:
[package]
name = "hello_cargo"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]

question.prompt_md: Which of these settings appear in the `[package]` section that `cargo new` writes? (Select all that apply.)

explanations.text_md: Correct. `name = "hello_cargo"` is the package name, taken from the `cargo new` command.
Correct. `version = "0.1.0"` is your project's own version number.
Correct. `edition = "2024"` says which edition of Rust the code is written in.
Not quite. Cargo finds `main` in `src/main.rs` by convention; there is no `main` setting in `Cargo.toml`.
Not quite. `rand` is a library. Libraries go under `[dependencies]`, not `[package]`, and a new project has none.

screens.heading: Build, then run

code.text:
$ cargo build
   Compiling hello_cargo v0.1.0 (/projects/hello_cargo)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.34s
$ ./target/debug/hello_cargo
Hello, world!
$ cargo run
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.00s
     Running `target/debug/hello_cargo`
Hello, world!

steps.caption_md: `cargo build` compiles the project. The executable goes in `target/debug/` (`hello_cargo.exe` on Windows), and Cargo creates `Cargo.lock` to record exact library versions.
steps.visual_md: Tree gains `Cargo.lock` (badge "new") and `target/` with `debug/` and `hello_cargo` inside (badges "new"; `hello_cargo` has a green border)

steps.caption_md: You can run the executable directly from `target/debug`.
steps.visual_md: `hello_cargo` executable node has the badge "running"

steps.caption_md: `cargo run` builds and runs in one command. Nothing changed since the last build, so Cargo skipped compiling. Most people just use `cargo run`.
steps.visual_md: Same tree; `hello_cargo` has the badge "running"; a note "not rebuilt: nothing changed" appears next to line 7

screens.visual_md: Code stepper (the folder tree from screen 2, which grows)

question.prompt_md: After `cargo build` in the `hello_cargo` project, the executable is in the folder `target/debug`.

explanations.text_md: Correct. Cargo keeps all build output in `target/`. A normal build is a debug build, so the executable is `target/debug/hello_cargo`.
Not quite. Unlike `rustc main.rs`, Cargo doesn't put the executable next to your source. It goes in `target/debug/`.

screens.heading: cargo check: does it still compile?
screens.text_md:
`cargo check` runs all the compiler's checks but skips making an executable. That makes it much faster than `cargo build`.

Use it while you write to check your code quickly. To run the program, use `cargo run`. The terminal transcripts show example paths and timings; those vary by machine.

code.text:
$ cargo check
    Checking hello_cargo v0.1.0 (/projects/hello_cargo)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.04s

question.prompt_md: You want to know quickly whether your project compiles, without making an executable. Which command do you use?

explanations.text_md: Not quite. `cargo new` creates a new project; it doesn't check existing code.
Not quite. `cargo build` checks the code too, but it also produces an executable, which takes longer.
Not quite. `cargo run` builds an executable and runs it. That's more than you asked for.
Correct. `cargo check` runs the compiler's checks and skips producing an executable, so it is usually faster than building.

left.label: With rustc

code.text:
$ rustc src/main.rs
$ ./main
Hello, world!

left.caption_md: Fine for a single file with no external libraries. You pick file names and run the result yourself.

right.label: With Cargo

code.text:
$ cargo run
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.00s
     Running `target/debug/hello_cargo`
Hello, world!

right.caption_md: Works the same for one file or a hundred, fetches libraries, and only recompiles what changed.

screens.heading: Cargo in this app
screens.text_md:
Single-file exercises can use `rustc` directly. Multi-file project exercises use Cargo and include a `Cargo.toml` and source files.

The app runs the tools locally: **Run** checks visible tests; **Submit** also checks hidden tests. You edit code here rather than typing terminal commands.

Outside the app, use the same Cargo commands yourself: `cargo new`, `cargo build`, `cargo run`, `cargo check`.

summary: **Cargo** is Rust's build tool and package manager; `cargo new name` creates a project.
`Cargo.toml` is the manifest: `[package]` has `name`, `version` and `edition`; `[dependencies]` lists libraries.
Your code lives in `src/main.rs`; build output goes in `target/`.
`cargo build` compiles, `cargo run` compiles and runs, `cargo check` only checks.
`Cargo.lock` records the exact versions of libraries; Cargo manages it for you.

questions.prompt_md: A computer's processor can run the Rust source text directly, without first translating it to machine code.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. Source code is text for people. The processor only runs machine code, so the source must be translated first.
Correct. The compiler, `rustc`, translates the source code into machine code, stored in an executable file.

questions.prompt_md: What is an **executable**?

options.text_md: The text file `main.rs` that you write.
A file of machine code that the computer can run, produced by the compiler.
The list of error messages the compiler prints.
The program that translates source code.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. `main.rs` is the source code. It's the compiler's input, not its output.
Correct. `rustc main.rs` writes an executable (`main`, or `main.exe` on Windows) that you can run as often as you like.
Not quite. Error messages appear only when compiling fails, and then no executable is made at all.
Not quite. That's the compiler, `rustc`. The executable is what the compiler produces.

Text that people write and read, such as `main.rs`

The tool that checks source code and translates it, such as `rustc`

questions.prompt_md: You compile `main.rs` with `rustc main.rs` and run `./main`; it prints `Hello`. You change the text in `main.rs` to `Goodbye`, save, and run `./main` again **without** compiling. What is printed?

options.text_md: Nothing: the executable deletes itself when the source changes.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. The executable is a separate file made from the old source. Changing `main.rs` doesn't change it until you compile again.
Correct. `./main` is still the old executable, which prints `Hello`. Run `rustc main.rs` again to get the new version.

problems.title: Menu card
problems.description_md:
A café prints its daily special from three values. The starter code gives you:

```rust
let dish = "Pancakes";
let price = 450;
let stars = 4;
```

Print exactly this card (9 lines):

```text
=========================
  Today's special
=========================
Dish: Pancakes
Price: 450 cents
Rating: 4 stars
Order code: {Pancakes-450}
To change the dish, edit {dish} in the code.
=========================
```

Rules:
- The `=` lines are 25 equals signs. Line 2 starts with **two spaces**.
- Every value (`Pancakes`, `450`, `4`) must come from a placeholder. **No digit** (`0`–`9`) may appear inside any string literal you pass to `print!` or `println!`, and neither may the word `Pancakes`.
- Print line 6 in two pieces: `print!` for `Rating: `, then `println!` for the rest.
- Line 7 wraps the dish and the price, joined by `-`, in real braces.
- Line 8 prints the **text** `{dish}`, not its value.

```
Output: "=========================

=========================
Dish: Pancakes
Price: 450 cents
Rating: 4 stars
Order code: {Pancakes-450}
To change the dish, edit {dish} in the code.
=========================
"
The whole card.

Input:  (no input)
Output line 7: "Order code: {Pancakes-450}"
Escaped braces right next to two placeholders.
```

- No digit and no `Pancakes` inside string literals passed to `print!`/`println!`.

hints: Count the lines and write one call per line, except line 6, which takes two calls. Escaped braces are `{{` and `}}`.
Line 7 is the tricky one: a literal `{`, the dish, a `-`, the price, then a literal `}`.

problems.title: Welcome banner
problems.description_md:
You're starting a program that you will grow through the whole course: a manager for the **Riverside Community Library**. By Chapter 21 it will lend books, charge late fees and answer web requests. Today it says hello.

Build the banner in two parts:

1. **Part 1 — Identity:** print the top border, the indented library name and the matching bottom border. Visible test 2 checks the name line; the hidden border tests check the frame.
2. **Part 2 — Opening hours:** add the hours as line 4. Visible test 1 checks the complete four-line result.

Write `main` so that the final program prints exactly these four lines:

```text
==============================
  Riverside Community Library
==============================
Open daily, 9:00 to 17:00
```

Details that matter:
- Lines 1 and 3 are exactly **30** equals signs (`=`).
- Line 2 starts with **two spaces**. Nothing comes after `Library`.
- Line 4 uses a colon in the times: `9:00` and `17:00`.
- Every line ends with a newline, and there is nothing else: no blank lines, no spaces at the ends of lines.

This file becomes `src/main.rs` of the library project. In Chapter 2 the banner stays, and a menu is added below it.

```
Input:  (no input)
Output: "==============================\n  Riverside Community Library\n==============================\nOpen daily, 9:00 to 17:00\n"
The whole banner.

Input:  (no input)
Output line 2: "  Riverside Community Library"
Two spaces first.
```

- The program reads no input.
- Use `println!` for the output.
hints: One `println!` per line. Copy the text carefully.
Count the `=` signs: 30. An easy way is to type 10, copy them, and paste twice more.
Line 2 is `println!("  Riverside Community Library");`, with the two spaces inside the quotes.
problems.solution_approach_md: Four `println!` calls: `"=============================="`, `"  Riverside Community Library"`, `"=============================="`, `"Open daily, 9:00 to 17:00"`. Note that `"9:00"` contains no braces, so no escaping is needed. The starter compiles, prints nothing and fails test 1.
problems.idiomatic_md: in later chapters the 30-character border becomes `"=".repeat(30)` (Chapter 4) and the times become constants, but for fixed text, plain `println!` calls are the clearest code.
